title: Deployment Case Study: Splitting the Payment Table
overview: This case splits Payment into ChequePayment and ApplePayPayment without a single disruptive cutover. Follow the lecture’s four stages: add tables, release code that reads both layouts, backfill historical data, then switch reads. The key reasoning is data compatibility: reducing live exposure with a canary does not itself preserve every rollback path.
big_ideas: Split a breaking schema change into additive structure, compatibility code, backfill and final read cutover.
Choose rolling for the additive schema stage and canary for behaviour changes, as in the lecture.
V1.1 writes new tables and reads them first, falling back to Payment for missing historical rows.
A retained old table preserves historical data, but does not contain new-only writes; a rollback plan must account for those.
Tombstone deletes so fallback and migration do not resurrect removed records.
Validate the migration and retain the compatible reader before switching to new-only reads.

sections.title: Scenario and constraints
sections.summary: Splitting a table is a breaking change, so it needs a multi-release plan.

items: **Payment** table currently holds all payment types
**Cheque** and **Apple Pay** capture different fields
So **Version 2** should write to **ChequePayment** and **ApplePayPayment** instead of Payment
**V2 cannot retrieve old Payment rows** until they are migrated
**Reverting to V1** can also hide payments written only to the new tables
**Schema expansion**
**Compatible code**
**Historical migration**
**Final read cutover**

terms.def: Marking a row as deleted without physically removing it.

check.q: V1 of the Payment service writes every payment to one Payment table; V2 will write cheque and Apple Pay payments to two new tables. Why is a direct switch from V1 to V2 unsafe?

items: **V2 cannot read the historical rows** that remain in Payment → old payments would vanish from its view
**Switching back to V1** hides the new payments V2 accepted only in the new tables
a.foot: Any plan has to keep **both historical and newly accepted payments readable** at every step, including **rollback**.

check.q: A teammate proposes doing the table split in a two-hour maintenance window with the service down, instead of the staged plan. When would that be acceptable, and what does the staged plan buy?

a.lead: **Acceptable if the customers can tolerate the downtime** and the window fits the migration.
items: The lecture's first question: **who are your customers?** **Banks or e-commerce** sites usually cannot
**Staged plan** keeps **payments flowing**
It gives a **rollback point at each step**
a.foot: **Cost**: several releases and **transitional code** that reads both layouts.

sections.title: Steps 1 and 2: new tables, then V1.1 canary
sections.summary: Add the tables, then canary V1.1 with new-table writes and fallback reads. Check the data needed by both versions before rolling back.

items: **Create ChequePayment and ApplePayPayment** without changing V1
Lecture chooses a **rolling update of database scripts**
**Dropping the unused new tables** reverses this step
That is **no longer harmless once they contain accepted payments**
**Write** new payments to the new tables
**Read** there first; **fall back to Payment** when absent
**Mark deletes with tombstones**
**Start with about 5–10% of transactions**, observe behaviour, then roll out
Lecture calls rollback **"okay"** → Payment is untouched and exposure is limited
This **preserves old rows**

sub: how **mixed V1/V1.1 instances** route reads of them

notes.foot: A complete plan must **resolve that compatibility gap** before using the canary in production.

check.q: Why does V1.1, which writes to the new tables and falls back to Payment for reads, go out as a canary rather than a straight rolling update?

items: **Canary** exposes only **5 to 10%** of transactions to the changed write and read behaviour
→ Problems show up on a **small surface** before wider rollout = limits the **blast radius**
It does **not** by itself make **rollback safe**
a.foot: Before relying on rollback, check how **V1** would see payments that **V1.1** wrote into the new tables.

check.q: A teammate proposes that V1.1 physically delete payment rows instead of tombstoning them. What would go wrong?

items: **Physical delete** from the new table → V1.1's **fallback read** finds the old row in Payment → the deleted payment **reappears**
A later **backfill** could copy it back
**Tombstone** marks the row as deleted → reads and the backfill know to **skip** it
a.foot: Every **reader and the backfill** must honour the marker for this to work.

check.q: During the canary, V1.1 records a payment only in ApplePayPayment. A later request for that payment reaches a V1 instance, which reads only Payment. What must the rollout plan address?

a.lead: V1 cannot find a payment that was accepted → the customer sees it as **missing**.
items: **Must address**: keep accepted payments **visible across mixed versions** and after any **rollback**
**Option**: keep a **reader that checks the new tables first**
**Option**: **limit where new-table writes are served** until every instance can read them
a.foot: Keeping **Payment untouched** and the **canary small** reduces exposure but does not solve this.

sections.title: Steps 3 and 4: migrate, then V1.2 becomes 2.0
sections.summary: Backfill old rows, validate the result, then canary new-only reads. Rollback should restore compatible reading without hiding new payments.

items: **Copy historical payments** into the new tables
**V1.1 continues** new-first, old-fallback reads
**Honour tombstones**
**Avoid overwriting newer data**
Lecture suggests **identifying migrated rows by updated date** for rollback → use only if it distinguishes migration copies from genuine new or changed payments
Only **after confirming all required historical rows are migrated**
**Canary V1.2**, roll it out, then **tag it 2.0**
**Rollback** → restore the **V1.1 compatible reader** if needed: it still reads new payments and falls back for old ones
**Returning to an old-only reader is unsafe** when new-only writes exist
**Retain data and the reader** needed by each rollback target
**Traffic strategies limit exposure**; they do **not reverse database writes**

check.q: The backfill copies old rows from Payment into the new tables while V1.1 is live. A payment was updated in the new table yesterday, and the backfill is about to copy its older version from Payment. What must the backfill do?

items: **Compare update dates** and skip rows that **already exist** in the new tables
Skip anything **tombstoned**
V1.1 keeps working during migration: it reads the **new tables first** and **falls back** only for missing rows
**Validate counts and samples** before moving on, because the next step stops reading Payment altogether

check.q: V1.2 reads only from the new tables. What makes rolling it back safe?

items: **V1.1** reads the new tables first and **falls back** to Payment for missing rows → **migrated and newly written** payments stay visible
**V1** would not: Payment lacks everything written since **cutover**
a.foot: So **V1.1 and the data it depends on** must be kept until V1.2 has proven itself.

check.q: Why does the case tag V1.2 as 2.0 rather than writing a fresh V2?

items: **V1.2 is already proven**: it has passed a **canary** and a rollout reading only the new tables
Tagging it avoids shipping a **new, untested build** at the **riskiest moment**
The **major version** marks the point where the old Payment table is **no longer part of the contract** = the **breaking change**

steps.label: 1. New tables
steps.detail: Add the two tables without changing V1. Drop them only while they contain no accepted payment data.

steps.label: 2. V1.1
steps.detail: Write new tables; read them first and fall back to Payment. Honour tombstones. Resolve mixed-version read compatibility before live rollout.

steps.label: 3. Migrate data
steps.detail: Copy historical rows without overwriting new changes or resurrecting deletes. Verify that migration copies can be distinguished from live data.

steps.label: 4. V1.2 = 2.0
steps.detail: After validating backfill, switch to new-only reads. Keep V1.1’s dual-layout reading available as the compatible rollback target.

exam_angles.q: Propose a near-zero-downtime plan to split an Orders table into two tables owned by different new schemas, and say how each step can be rolled back.

items.t: **Step 1: add the new tables only**, with no code change

sub: Writes new orders to the **new tables**
Make sure every version that can serve traffic, or be **rolled back to**, can still **see new-table orders**

items.t: **Step 4: canary a release that reads only the new tables**
sub: Keep the **compatibility release** as the **rollback target**
Then **tag it as the new major version**

exam_angles.q: Why is canary preferred over blue/green for the transitional version in the Payment case, and what does neither strategy solve?

items: **Canary** exposes only a **small share of transactions** to the changed data behaviour → problems surface **before full rollout**; needs **no second environment**
**Blue/green** switches **all traffic at once**; it switches back quickly, but **every user** hits the new data path at the same moment
a.foot: **Neither** undoes writes to the **shared database** or makes them readable by old code → the **compatibility plan** (dual reads, tombstones, a retained reader) is still required.

exam_angles.q: A teammate's plan for the Payment split is: (1) canary V2, which writes and reads only the new tables, at 10%; (2) migrate the old data; (3) roll out V2. Critique the plan and correct it.

sub: **During step 1**: V2 cannot see **historical payments**, and V1 instances cannot see payments **V2 accepted** → customers on both sides see **missing payments**
**Rolling back** loses visibility of V2's writes
**Canary V1.1** with new-table writes, **fallback reads** and **tombstones**
**Canary V1.2** reading only the new tables → **tag it as 2.0**

a.foot: Each step stays **backward compatible** with the one before.

exam_angles.q: How is rollback handled at each stage of the Payment case, and where does the lecture's shortcut need more design?

items: **Step 1**: drop the **unused new tables**
**Step 2**: stop the **V1.1 rollout**, but **keep every payment it accepted**, since V1 alone may not read them
**Step 3**: if needed, remove only **migrated copies** identified by **updated date**, never live changes
**Step 4**: go back to **V1.1's new-first, old-fallback reader**
a.foot: **Shortcut gap**: the lecture says canary rollback is fine because **Payment is untouched**, but that misses payments written to the **new tables** in the meantime → **reconciliation** and **mixed-version reads** still need designing.
